transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-10-20
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Daniel Ortiz (Redwood SE), Aisha Patel (Luminary CTO), Ben Cho (Luminary ML Eng), Sara Levy (Luminary SRE), Marc Diaz (Product), Olga Kim (Procurement)

Summary:
This was a PoC scoping call to align on success criteria for a 4-week POC to evaluate Redwood's inference economics for Luminary's customer support triage model (seq len ~512 tokens, avg request size 400 tokens, 5M monthly queries). Primary ask: detailed per-token cost modeling with batching and prefix/KV caching knobs, and a benchmark plan to validate throughput/latency under realistic traffic. Luminary is leaning toward a dedicated/private deployment if unit economics and security checks clear. Next steps: Redwood to send pricing & SOW, bench plan, Luminary to provide query histograms and sample prompts.

Topics Covered:
- Current stack and constraints (on-prem vs cloud, data residency)
- Workload sizing (qps, concurrency, avg/95th token counts)
- Benchmark plan (dataset, perf metrics, envs to test: hosted vs dedicated vs private)
- Cost modeling (per-token estimates, batching, KV cache hit assumptions)
- Security/compliance pre-reqs for private deployment (KMS, audit logs)
- Timeline and procurement triggers

Action items (also above): listed for owners and due dates.

Transcript (imperfect automatic transcription, occasional mislabels):
[00:00] Maya Chen: Alright, good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining, we'll kick off in a minute. Uh this is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on this account. With me is Danny, Daniel Ortiz, our solutions engineer.
[00:12] Daniel Ortiz: Hey everyone, hi, thanks for the time. I'll jump into the perf and cost bits later.
[00:17] Aisha Patel: Hi, thanks, appreciate it. Wanted to make sure we can cover the cost modeling and whether it makes sense for us to go dedicated or private. We have compliance concerns and also a pretty tight cost envelope.
[00:30] Ben Cho: Yeah hi, Ben here. Quick note on the workload - we're doing support triage, average prompt about 400 tokens, with some longer follow-ups. Roughly 5 million queries per month, but spiky - weekdays 9-6 are heavy.
[00:45] Sara Levy: We also care about 95th pct latency under 300 ms for interactive UI. Bulk jobs can be higher but this is customer facing.
[00:55] Maya Chen: Great, that's the key bit. So for the POC we usually run a 2-4 week bench, we can do hosted first for speed then show Dedicated numbers; private requires a little more setup. We should define success criteria, budget, and the dataset.
[01:10] Marc Diaz: On success criteria we'd want: cost per successful triage under $0.01, 95th lat under 300ms for 1-request flows, and no PII leakage — which we'll validate via our eval set.
[01:25] Daniel Ortiz: Okay, quick framing on cost modeling — there are three knobs: batching, KV/prefix cache hit, and quantization/model choice. For a 400-token average payload, batching can increase throughput but adds tail latency. The math we use: cost_per_token = (GPU-hour cost / tokens_per_hour) + infra admin. But I'll put exact numbers in the deck.
[01:50] Ben Cho: Can you give a ballpark now? Like per-token cost for hosted vs dedicated?
[01:55] Daniel Ortiz: Ballpark, assuming a modern 70B open model quantized to 4-bit and moderate batching, you might be in the $0.0008 to $0.002 per token range for hosted depending on load. Dedicated can drop that ~20-40% but you'll have a commit. These are rough, will refine once we have qps and cache hit rate.
[02:14] Aisha Patel: That spread matters. Our finance team is pushing for sub $0.01 per triage (so roughly 400 tokens * x should be under that).
[02:25] Maya Chen: Right, so for Luminary's 400 tokens target, to hit $0.01 per request you need an average token cost <= $0.000025 — which is tight; I think Marc's $0.01 per triage might assume shorter effective generation. We should double-check assumptions — are you counting input+output tokens?
[02:45] Marc Diaz: Good point, we meant end-to-end cost including generation and embeddings step for reranking as well. So maybe we need to break it out: triage classification step vs full generation.
[02:58] Daniel Ortiz: Yeah that matters. Also, KV cache helps a lot for multi-turn flows — if you have a 30% cache hit on prefixes that reduces tokens sent to model. Batching: if you batch to 8-16 requests, you amortize overhead but tail latency increases. Redwood has adaptive batching that respects SLOs, we can tune the target percentiles.
[03:20] Ben Cho: Our traffic is pretty spiky - peak qps ~120, baseline ~10. We can share histograms.
[03:28] Sara Levy: Also, ops question — if we go private we need KMS integration, audit logs, and RBAC. Can Redwood support HSM/KMS and long-term audit retention?
[03:39] Daniel Ortiz: Yes — private supports KMS/HSM, we can stream audit logs to your SIEM, RBAC via SSO/SAML. We'll include compliance appendix in the SOW.
[03:48] Olga Kim: Procurement wants to know procurement triggers — like thresholds that flip from PoC to reserved capacity.
[03:54] Maya Chen: We typically see customers start with a 4-week PoC and then move to a 3-12 month reserved if cost and perf meet targets. We can include pricing brackets in the proposal.
[04:05] Aisha Patel: Benchmark plan — what will you run?
[04:08] Daniel Ortiz: Plan: 1) Replay of real traffic (you provide histogram + sample prompts), 2) synthetic stress focusing on 95th percentile, 3) cold vs warm KV cache scenarios. We'll test hosted (fastest to run) and at least one dedicated perf number and estimate private deployment cost. We'll measure throughput (qps per GPU), p50/p95/p99 latency, and token cost.
[04:30] Ben Cho: How long to run the bench? We need both steady-state and peak windows.
[04:34] Daniel Ortiz: We recommend a 2-4 hour steady state and several spike tests; overall bench execution for Redwood side can be done in 3 business days once we have the samples and access. But private setup might take 2-3 weeks because of networking/KMS.
[04:48] Marc Diaz: What's your assumption on GPU type? A100? H100? Cost delta?
[04:52] Daniel Ortiz: For hosted numbers we usually use a cost model equivalent to A100. Dedicated/private can be H100 or A100 depending on what's provisioned; H100s increase perf but also per-hour costs. We'll give cost per GPU-hour and per-token under different inst types.
[05:05] Aisha Patel: We'll want a sensitivity table — e.g., cost per token under cache hit rates 0/20/50% and batching sizes 1/8/16.
[05:15] Maya Chen: Absolutely — that's part of the cost model we'll send. Also note that Redwood Optimize recommendations can suggest quantization and batching settings for your workload to hit a target cost.
[05:25] Ben Cho: For the POC data, can we mask PII before sending? We have legal constraints with customer text.
[05:30] Maya Chen: Yes — you can send a sampled masked dataset or we can run a local private bench if needed.
[05:36] Sara Levy: On monitoring, we'll need per-token cost dashboards, per-route latency, and tracing for tail events. Does the console expose token-level breakdown?
[05:45] Daniel Ortiz: Yeah Redwood Console has token-level cost and latency breakdowns, route-level dashboards, and tracing hooks. We can show you an example during the follow-up demo.
[05:54] Olga Kim: On procurement timing — if the PoC shows savings we'll likely want to start procurement immediately. Need estimated lead times for reserved capacity purchase.
[06:02] Maya Chen: Reserved capacity lead time varies, often 2-4 weeks post-contract for provisioning. We can include expedite options in the proposal.
[06:10] Aisha Patel: Can you summarize assumptions you'll use for cost model?
[06:14] Daniel Ortiz: Sure, we'll assume: model family and size (you pick or we recommend), quantization level (4-bit int8/4-bit), cache hit rates scenarios (0/20/50%), batching strategies (no batch, batch=8, batch=16), GPU types (A100/H100), and duty cycles (steady vs peak). We'll output per-token, per-request, and monthly burn for your 5M queries baseline.
[06:38] Ben Cho: For our math, we'd like to see a table: tokens per GPU-hour, cost per GPU-hour, token tech overhead, and network/infra overhead.
[06:48] Daniel Ortiz: Yep, we'll enumerate tokens/hour numbers for typical models. Quick off-the-cuff: a quantized 70B on an A100 might do X tokens per second — I'll get precise numbers.
[06:58] Aisha Patel: Security review — we'll need SOC2 and ISO, and we'd like to do a short architecture review.
[07:04] Maya Chen: We can share SOC2 cert and our security pack; Daniel can join a security deep-dive next week if you'd like.
[07:12] Marc Diaz: Timeline thought: sample data by Friday (10/23), Redwood bench plan and SOW by Sunday (10/22) wait that's earlier — ok SOW by 10/22, bench plan by 10/25, execute bench the week of 10/26, follow-up the week of 11/2. Procurement in parallel.
[07:28] Olga Kim: That aligns with our procurement calendar.
[07:33] Maya Chen: Great, I'll send the SOW and draft pricing later today/tomorrow. Any other open Qs?
[07:39] Sara Levy: One nit — how do you handle model fallbacks if dedicated capacity is saturated? We need graceful degradation.
[07:45] Daniel Ortiz: Smart routing — we can failover to hosted or a smaller model variant and return a header indicating fallback. We'll define policies in the SOW.
[07:55] Ben Cho: Also, embedding costs for reranking — include that as a separate line item in the model.
[07:59] Daniel Ortiz: Yep, embeddings and rerank will be separate in the cost table.
[08:04] Maya Chen: Cool. We'll wrap — I'll send follow ups. Thanks everybody.

Recap / Next steps (auto-summary style):
- Redwood to send draft SOW + pricing by 2026-10-22 (Maya).
- Redwood to share benchmark plan and GPU-hour estimates by 2026-10-25 (Daniel).
- Luminary to share query histograms, sample prompts, and security contacts by 2026-10-23 (Aisha/Ben).
- Schedule benchmark execution week of 2026-10-26 and follow-up demo weeks of 2026-10-26 or 2026-11-02.

References mentioned:
- Example benchmark spreadsheet (link sent in chat)
- Security pack / SOC2 docs (to be shared)

End of transcript.
